638.title: The Khalsa's greeting
638.hook: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh: the Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory
638.howItsDone: Sikhs greet one another, and open talks in the gurdwara, with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; the listener replies with the same words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jaikara, and your line: sat sri akaal. Today, a second Sikh greeting, longer, with a twist at the end.

A speaker steps up to the microphone in a gurdwara. Before a single word of the talk, they put their palms together and say: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. And the whole congregation says it straight back to them, word for word. Only then does the talk begin. Two friends meet at the door afterward and say the same thing, sometimes shortened to just fateh. It sounds like a formality. It's actually a small statement about who wins.
screen: `A SPEAKER AT THE MICROPHONE.` → `THE HALL SAYS IT BACK.` → `A STATEMENT ABOUT WHO WINS.`

segments.voice: Take the two halves. Waheguru ji ka Khalsa: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru. The Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs that Guru Gobind Singh founded at Anandpur on Vaisakhi in 1699, and tradition explains the word khalsa as pure, belonging directly to the sovereign with no middleman. Then Waheguru ji ki fateh: the victory belongs to Waheguru. Fateh means victory. Sikh tradition links this greeting to the founding of the Khalsa, and the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, gives it as the greeting Sikhs use with one another. Now, the twist. A greeting about victory could easily turn into bragging: we win. This one does the opposite. It hands the victory away the moment it's spoken. Whatever goes well, the exam, the deal, the hard conversation, the battle in older times, the greeting says it isn't the speaker's. It's Waheguru's. And the people saying it don't belong to themselves either. So two people greeting each other this way remind each other, every time, of two things: you are not your own, and the credit is not yours. That could sound heavy. Some Sikhs describe it as freeing instead: if the victory is God's, then so, in a way, is the pressure. A person can work as hard as they're able, then let the outcome rest where it belongs. And it's said back, word for word. Neither person is above the other in this greeting. Both are equally God's.
screen: `THE KHALSA: FOUNDED 1699.` · `KHALSA: BELONGING TO GOD.` · `FATEH: VICTORY.` · `HANDING THE VICTORY AWAY.` · then, large: `THE VICTORY IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that went well for you recently, something you might be quietly proud of, and picture it clearly. Without dismissing your effort, imagine handing the credit forward, to the people who helped, to the chances you were given, and, if you pray, to the One, and notice whether that feels like a loss or a relief. If you're comfortable, say the greeting once, softly: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh.
Fateh. Victory. In the Khalsa's greeting, Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, both the community and the victory belong to God.
Your line: the victory is his. Said back, word for word, between equals. Day six hundred thirty-eight.

639.title: Ardas before a meal
639.hook: families say a short Ardas before eating, and in the gurdwara food is offered with an Ardas before it's served
639.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, langar and karah prashad are offered with an Ardas before being served; at home, Sikh families often say a short Ardas or simply Waheguru before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fateh: the victory belongs to Waheguru, and so do the people who say it. This week the Ardas leaves the gurdwara hall and comes home, starting at the table.

The plates are down. The dal is steaming, the rotis are stacked under a cloth, and someone's younger brother already has one hand moving. In a Sikh home, that hand often gets a gentle look: wait. Someone stands, or just folds their hands at the table, and says a short Ardas, sometimes only a few lines, sometimes just Waheguru and a thank-you. Then everyone eats. It takes less than a minute.
screen: `THE DAL IS STEAMING.` → `ONE HAND ALREADY MOVING.` → `WAIT: A SHORT ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas we've been walking through line by line is long. But it isn't only for the gurdwara, and it isn't only the full form: Sikhs pray it short when the moment is short. Before food, the idea is simple. Thank the Giver before taking the gift. In the gurdwara, this is done with care. Before langar is served, food from the kitchen is often brought before the Guru Granth Sahib and an Ardas is said over it. Karah prashad, the sweet offering everyone receives, is blessed with an Ardas too, and a kirpan is often touched to it before it's shared. Earlier in this stretch, fateh named the cooking pot in the same breath as the sword; a meal Ardas brings that pot home to a single table. At home it's simpler, and families vary: a few lines, a quiet Waheguru, a moment of folded hands. What stays the same is the pause. The food is treated as given, not just bought. And the pause changes the meal. A plate you've given thanks for is hard to waste, and harder to eat in a rush or in front of a screen. It reminds the table that somewhere, a langar is serving strangers the same dal.

segments.voice: Picture the next plate you'll eat from, and trace it back: the field, the truck, the store, the hands that cooked it, even if those hands were yours. Let one face come to mind among all those people, and let yourself feel grateful, plainly, without needing the right words. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or a line you already know.

Karah prashad, the sweet offering blessed with an Ardas and shared with everyone: before langar is served, food is brought before the Guru Granth Sahib for an Ardas, and families pause at home too, before eating.
Your line: thanks before food. Short or long, the Ardas fits the moment. Day six hundred thirty-nine, done.

640.title: Ardas before a journey
640.hook: before travel, exams or new work, Sikhs ask for help in Ardas
640.howItsDone: Before travel, exams, a new job or another undertaking, Sikhs often say a short Ardas at home or ask for one at the gurdwara, sometimes offering karah prashad, asking that the task be brought to a good end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, and the pause before food: thanks to the Giver before the gift. Today the Ardas walks out the front door with you.

The suitcase is zipped. The ride is two minutes away. A student has an exam at nine; someone starts a new job on Monday and hasn't slept well all weekend. In some Sikh families, before anyone walks out, hands fold and a short Ardas is said, sometimes by a grandparent, sometimes by the traveler. Sometimes the family goes to the gurdwara first and asks for the Ardas there. Then, and only then, the door opens.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IS ZIPPED.` → `AN EXAM AT NINE.` → `HANDS FOLD BEFORE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Every full Ardas already asks for this. Near the end comes the line sarbat de kaaraj raas karne: make everyone's tasks succeed. Kaaraj is a task, an undertaking. Raas means set right, brought to a good end. It's a general request, for everybody. Before a journey, an exam, a wedding, a surgery or a new business, Sikhs make it specific: this trip, this test, this first day. Families sometimes offer karah prashad at the gurdwara so the Ardas can be said there, with the congregation joining in. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib fits these moments. In Sri Rag ki Var, on ang 91, it says, in effect: whatever work you want done, speak of it to the Lord; the True Guru will set it right, and you have His word on it. Notice what this asking isn't. It isn't a lucky charm, and it isn't a way to skip the studying. Sikh teaching expects honest effort: you still pack, still prepare, still drive carefully. In the Ardas, effort and outcome come in order: the work is done, the result is placed in the hands of the One, and then the traveler goes. And saying a task out loud means naming what you're really walking into: this is the road, this is what I hope for, this is in Your hands.

segments.voice: Think of your very next real task, a call, a drive, a meeting, and picture the doorway you'll cross to get to it. On the in-breath, see yourself doing the work honestly and well; on the out-breath, let go of how it turns out. If you pray, you can place it before the One in your own words, or simply say Waheguru.

641.title: Ardas in grief
641.hook: the Ardas for the dead asks peace for the one who has gone, and for those left, the strength to accept the Will
641.howItsDone: After a death, Sikhs sing Kirtan Sohila at the cremation, often hold a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and close it with an Ardas asking rest for the departed and acceptance of the Will for the family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaaraj: name the task, do your part, and ask that it come to a good end. Today, the hardest door the Ardas walks through. Go gently.

A family stands in a gurdwara a few days after a funeral. Some of them haven't slept. Someone holds a framed photo; someone else holds a toddler who doesn't understand why everyone is so quiet. In the days since the death, the Guru Granth Sahib has been read, perhaps from beginning to end. Now the reading is finished. The congregation rises, and the Ardas begins. Somewhere in it, the name of the one who died is spoken aloud, for the last time in this way.
screen: `A FAMILY, A FEW DAYS AFTER.` → `THE READING IS FINISHED.` → `THE NAME IS SPOKEN ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Sikhs usually cremate their dead, and Kirtan Sohila, the evening hymns, is sung at the cremation. Over the following days, families often hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, and when it ends, an Ardas is said that is often called the antim ardas, the final prayer. It asks two things. For the one who has gone: that their soul find rest, a place at the Guru's feet, union with the One. And for the ones left: the strength to accept the Will. That word, will, is bhaana, and it runs all through Sikh teaching. Bhaana mannan, accepting the Will, is honored, and it is hard. Guru Arjan put it in a single line. In Raag Asa, on ang 394, he says, in effect: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. An honest note. Accepting the Will doesn't mean pretending it doesn't hurt. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing and ritual displays of mourning, and treats death as part of the One's order rather than a punishment. But it doesn't forbid tears. Acceptance is something people grow into, sometimes over years, and the Ardas doesn't demand it be finished by Sunday; it asks for the strength to keep moving toward it. And the family isn't asked to do this alone. The whole congregation stands with them, and the line rising spirits, good for all, is said even here.
screen: `KIRTAN SOHILA AT THE CREMATION.` · `REST FOR THE ONE WHO HAS GONE.` · `BHAANA: THE WILL.` · `ACCEPTANCE TAKES TIME.` · then, large: `IN HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: Take this at whatever depth feels right today: bring to mind someone you miss, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, or someone who isn't gone but is far away, and if it hurts, let it hurt a little. Breathe. If you pray, you can ask peace for them, and the strength to accept what you can't change, with a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply wish them peace.
Bhaana, the Will of the One: after a death, the Ardas asks rest for the one who has gone, and for the family, the strength to accept it.

642.title: Ardas in joy
642.hook: births, weddings and new homes all get an Ardas of thanks
642.howItsDone: Sikhs mark births, weddings, new homes and other blessings with a shukrana, an Ardas of thanks, often with a reading, karah prashad and the singing of Anand Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhaana: in grief, the Ardas asks for strength to accept the Will. Today, the same prayer at the opposite end of life's weather.

When do you reach for something bigger more often: when things are falling apart, or when they're going well? Trouble tends to send people looking. Good news tends to go to the group chat. Sikh life has a deliberate counterweight. A baby is born: an Ardas. A wedding: an Ardas at the start and at the end. A new home, a new shop, a new job that finally came through: an Ardas. Not asking for anything. Just saying thank you.
screen: `WHEN DO YOU REACH UPWARD?` → `TROUBLE SENDS US LOOKING.` → `GOOD NEWS GETS AN ARDAS TOO.`

segments.voice: Punjabi has a word for this: shukrana, thanksgiving. A shukrane di ardas is a prayer of thanks, the same frame as every Ardas, with the petition turned into gratitude. Look at how joy gets marked. When a baby is born, the family often brings the child to the gurdwara. An Ardas of thanks is said, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the hymn on that page, the hukamnama, guides the choice of the child's name. A wedding, the Anand Karaj, begins with an Ardas; the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib four times, and it ends with an Ardas again. In a new home, many families hold a reading, often of Sukhmani Sahib, and close it with an Ardas, sometimes with karah prashad for everyone who came. You'll often hear Anand Sahib too, the song of bliss by Guru Amar Das, on ang 917. It opens, in effect: joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. The Rehat Maryada has it sung at weddings and other ceremonies, and a short portion is recited near the close of congregational gatherings. Why make such a point of thanks? In Sikh teaching, the good things are gifts from the One just as surely as the hard things are within the Will. Grief is met with acceptance; joy is met with gratitude. Both keep the eyes on the Giver, not only on the gift.
screen: `SHUKRANA: THANKSGIVING.` · `A BIRTH: A NAME FROM THE HUKAM.` · `A WEDDING BEGINS AND ENDS IN ARDAS.` · `ANAND SAHIB: JOY HAS COME.` · then, large: `THANKS IN JOY.`

Instead of moving on, stay with it. If you pray, you can thank the One for it in your own words or with a single Waheguru; if not, simply hold the gratitude without asking for anything more.

643.title: Why standing
643.hook: the Ardas is said standing: readiness and respect, like standing before a king
643.howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas with hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, often after reciting 'tu thakur tum peh ardaas' from Sukhmani Sahib; those who cannot stand join seated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukrana: joy gets an Ardas too, a thank-you with nothing added. Today, not the words of the Ardas but the body that says them.

A judge walks into a courtroom and everyone rises. A national anthem starts and a stadium stands up, even the people holding nachos. In some classrooms, a teacher walks in and the whole room gets to its feet. Standing is an old way of saying: this matters, and I'm paying attention. In the gurdwara, when it's time for the Ardas, the whole congregation stands. Hands are folded. Faces turn toward the Guru Granth Sahib. Nobody needs to be told why.
screen: `ALL RISE.` → `A STADIUM ON ITS FEET.` → `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas is often called the standing prayer, and Sikhs give a few reasons for the posture that fit together. The first is respect. Sikhs speak of the Guru as the true king, sacha paatshah. The picture is a royal court, where a petition was presented standing, hands joined, and the Ardas, a petition, is made the same way before the Guru Granth Sahib. The second is readiness. Someone sitting is resting; someone standing can move. Sikh history remembers people who stood up for others, and the posture keeps that in the body: whatever is asked for, the one asking is ready to act on it. The third is togetherness. When everyone stands, nobody is above anyone else. The grandmother and the teenager, the regular and the first-time visitor, are on their feet side by side. Just before the Ardas, a line from Sukhmani Sahib, on ang 268, is often recited. It says, in effect: You are the Master, to You is this prayer; body and soul are all Your gift. It sets the tone: not a list of demands, but servants presenting themselves. And one thing, plainly. The posture is a custom of respect, not a test. People who can't stand, the elderly, the sick, someone with a baby asleep on their lap, join the Ardas sitting, and they're no less part of it. Standing is what the heart is doing. The legs just help when they can.
screen: `RESPECT: BEFORE THE TRUE KING.` · `READINESS: READY TO ACT.` · `TOGETHERNESS: NOBODY ABOVE.` · `ANG 268: YOU ARE THE MASTER.` · then, large: `STAND READY.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand up now, feet a little apart, hands folded in front of your chest if you like; if you can't stand, sit up tall and let your spine do the standing. Notice whether it feels different from sitting: more awake, maybe, or more ready. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing, and let that be your whole prayer for now.
Why standing. The Ardas is said standing, hands joined: respect before the true king, readiness to act, and everyone equal on their feet.
Your line: stand ready. Respect, readiness, and nobody above anyone else. Day six hundred forty-three, counted.

644.title: Your own petition
644.hook: putting a short personal request into your own words, the way Sikhs do inside the Ardas
644.howItsDone: Sikhs place their own request into the Ardas at the petition, in Punjabi or any language; at home a person praying alone names their reason in their own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why standing: respect, readiness, and nobody above anyone else. Today the week ends with the most personal part of the Ardas.

Most of the Ardas is inherited. The words about the ten Gurus, the martyrs, vichhora, rising spirits and good for all come down through generations, the same in a village in Punjab and a suburb in California. But there's one part no one can write for you: the petition, the reason today. It can be said in Punjabi, in English, in a whisper, in the words of a seven-year-old asking for her cat to get better. And it's still Ardas.
screen: `MOST OF THE ARDAS IS INHERITED.` → `ONE PART NO ONE CAN WRITE FOR YOU.` → `IN ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Sikh teaching doesn't treat personal asking as something embarrassing. Guru Nanak says it plainly in the Japji, in the fourth pauri, on ang 2: we speak, we beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. The asking is expected. What Sikhs often add is a sense of how to ask. A petition is called a benti, a humble request: not a demand, not a bargain, not a list of grievances. Think back over this week. Fateh: the victory belongs to God, so no one has to pretend to control the outcome. Karah prashad: begin with thanks. Before a journey: name the task honestly. In grief: ask for the strength to accept the Will, not only for the pain to stop. In joy: thanks, with nothing added. Standing: come ready to act on what you ask. Put those together and you have something like a shape for a personal petition, without anyone handing you the words. First, what you're thankful for. Then what you're asking, plainly. Then who else it's for, because the Ardas always widens. Some Sikhs also add a line of acceptance, that whatever comes is within the Will. The words themselves are yours, and nobody grades them. An Ardas said in clumsy English by a teenager at 2 a.m. is still Ardas. An honest, clumsy benti fits that word better than a beautiful one that isn't meant.
screen: `WE BEG, AND THE GIVER GIVES.` · `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `THANKS, ASK, WIDEN, ACCEPT.` · `CLUMSY AND HONEST IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Compose three lines, in your head or in your phone's notes: something you're thankful for today, the one thing you most want to ask for, and someone else this is for. Don't polish them or make them sound holy; just make them true. If you pray, you can offer them inside your own prayer or after a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply read them back to yourself.
Benti, a humble request: inside the inherited Ardas, the reason for today is said in your own words, in any language.
Your line: your own words. Clumsy and honest is enough for a benti. See you next time.
